say: Circling the giant planet Jupiter, there is a small world wrapped in ice.
Its name is Europa.
Scientists believe a hidden ocean lies beneath that crust, holding more than twice the water in all of Earth's seas.
And now, the James Webb Space Telescope has found carbon dioxide on its surface, in a spot that seems to point straight down to that ocean.
Europa is slightly smaller than our own Moon, about three thousand one hundred kilometres across.
Its surface is water ice, crisscrossed by cracks and ridges, and colder than anywhere on Earth: far below minus one hundred degrees Celsius.
Jupiter's radiation floods the surface, enough to give an astronaut a lethal dose within hours.
Not exactly a place you would expect to look for life.
But the surface is only the outer layer of the story.
To get a sense of scale: Europa is about a quarter of Earth's width, and just a little smaller than the Moon.
Yet it may hold twice as much water as Earth.
Europa has a metal core, a rocky mantle, and above them, a global ocean of salty liquid water.
Estimates put the ice shell at roughly fifteen to thirty kilometres thick, and the ocean beneath it at sixty to a hundred and fifty kilometres deep.
That is many times deeper than any ocean on Earth, and it wraps the entire moon.
The layers here are not to scale.
This ocean may have existed for billions of years, hidden under a roof of ice.
So what keeps that ocean from freezing solid?
Tides.
Europa is locked in a rhythm with its neighbours Io and Ganymede. For every orbit of Ganymede, Europa orbits twice, and Io four times.
That gravitational tug of war keeps squeezing and flexing Europa, and the friction deep inside produces heat.
Life as we know it needs a few things: liquid water, a source of energy, and the right chemical ingredients.
Europa may have the water. Tidal heating could supply the energy.
But carbon, the backbone of life on Earth, had never been traced back to Europa's ocean.
Enter the James Webb Space Telescope.
Its main mirror is six and a half metres wide, made of eighteen gold-coated hexagonal segments.
A five-layer sunshield, as big as a tennis court, keeps its instruments colder than minus two hundred degrees Celsius.
Webb sees infrared light, heat, which is exactly what we need to read the chemistry of icy worlds.
It orbits a point called L2, about one and a half million kilometres from Earth, always shielded from the Sun's glare.
In its early observations, Webb pointed its Near-Infrared Spectrograph at Europa.
Instead of taking a simple photo, this instrument splits the light from every pixel into a spectrum.
Different molecules absorb light at different wavelengths, leaving fingerprints in that spectrum.
Europa is only about ten pixels across, each covering a few hundred kilometres, but that is enough.
And it took only a few minutes of observing time.
The fingerprint appeared near four point two seven microns: the unmistakable signature of carbon dioxide ice.
And it was not spread evenly.
The carbon dioxide was concentrated in one region: Tara Regio, a patch of jumbled, broken ice about eighteen hundred kilometres across.
Scientists call this chaos terrain, a landscape where the ice shell has been shattered, with blocks of ice tilted and frozen in place.
A weaker signal also showed up in a neighbouring chaos region, Powys Regio.

Two independent teams, led by Geronimo Villanueva at NASA Goddard and Samantha Trumbo at Cornell, reached the same conclusion, in papers published in Science on the twenty-first of September, twenty twenty-three.
Here is what that terrain might look like up close. An artist's visualisation, not a photograph.
Rafts of ice, broken apart and refrozen, with Jupiter hanging huge in the black sky.
In places like this, the ice shell may have been disrupted by material rising from below.
But where did the carbon come from?
Carbon dioxide is not stable on Europa's surface, so it must have arrived geologically recently.
It could have been delivered by meteorites, or made on the surface by radiation.
But its concentration in young terrain, and the lack of complex organic molecules in the data, point to an internal source: the ocean.
Add Hubble's detection of table salt in the same region, in twenty nineteen, and the picture hangs together.
None of this proves life. Webb saw no sign of water plumes, though that does not rule them out.
And carbon dioxide alone says nothing about biology.
A twenty twenty-six analysis of Webb data suggests it may extend across more of Europa's chaos terrain than first thought.
The next chapters belong to spacecraft.
NASA's Europa Clipper launched in October twenty twenty-four, and swings past Earth in December twenty twenty-six for a final gravity assist.
It reaches Jupiter in April twenty thirty, and will make around fifty close flybys of Europa.
ESA's Juice follows, with two Europa flybys planned for July twenty thirty-two.
Together they will map Europa's ice, and test whether the ocean really connects to its surface.
Webb did not find life on Europa. But it gave us a map, pointing to where the ocean may reach the surface.
Would you be surprised if there is life under that ice? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more.
Beneath the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa hides an ocean with twice the water of all Earth's seas.
Warmed by tides, that ocean may have stayed liquid for billions of years.
Now, the James Webb Space Telescope has looked at its icy surface in infrared.
And it found carbon dioxide, concentrated in one region of shattered ice called Tara Regio. Carbon is a key ingredient for life, and this suggests it came up from the ocean below.
Because that ice is young, and carbon dioxide does not last, it was probably delivered recently, from below.
Is there life down there? Europa Clipper arrives in twenty thirty to find out. Follow for more.
